entries.title: The Los Angeles Rams Are Trying to Defeat Time
entries.summary: Welcome to the Super Bowl of jet lag.
entries.content:
Usually, when the San Francisco 49ers and the Los Angeles Rams play, it’s a relatively short commute. But this evening, the teams will kick off the NFL’s first-ever regular-season game in Australia.

The two teams have taken diametrically opposite approaches to preventing the 8,000-mile journey from disorienting their stars. The 49ers boarded their 16-hour flight to Melbourne nine days ago and have spent the intervening time training, watching Aussie rules football, and winning the majority of local support. The Rams landed yesterday, just 24 hours before the game. They’re betting on being in Australia so briefly that players’ brains and bodies won’t notice the difference. That makes the game the most high-profile test of jet-lag-evasion techniques in American sports history.

Anyone who has hurled across several time zones in one go knows how wide-awake and helplessly sleepy you can feel at inappropriate hours upon landing—a major inconvenience for professional football players, whose career depends on how they perform during one very specific period. Circadian rhythms can also affect performance in less obvious ways. Compounds that encourage inflammation, for instance, spike at night, when the body is doing less and can direct more energy toward fighting infection. A new time zone throws that optimal function off tilt and can cause stomach issues, cognitive impairment, headaches, and mood changes.

Teams at a circadian disadvantage tend to play worse. One study that analyzed every NFL game from 1970 to 2011 with a kickoff after 8 p.m. ET found that West Coast teams did better than oddsmakers expected in two out of every three games, regardless of whether they were home or away. Head coaches are also more likely to make the risky call to attempt an offensive play on a fourth down during evening games when they travel west compared with any other direction.

Because the consequences of jet lag are well established, the real question is how to avoid them. In 2021, 26 sleep researchers and clinicians articulated their best answer in the journal Sports Medicine. Among other recommendations, they noted that fully recovering from jet lag takes one day for each time zone crossed. The 49ers seem to have followed that model by leaving more than a week ahead of the game. (Melbourne is 17 hours ahead of California, but for body-clock purposes, that’s the same as being seven hours behind.) Kyle Shanahan, the 49ers’ head coach, told reporters last month that he would have loved to have just shown up in Australia the day before but that the experts he’d spoken with had all recommended arriving earlier. “I was a little bit on the fence,” he said. “Science wasn’t.”

The Rams, by contrast, are attempting to not switch their body clock at all. They have spent the past few weeks practicing in the late afternoon, which aligns with Friday’s mid-morning kickoff in Melbourne. Their head coach, Sean McVay, said at a Sunday press conference that the team will “have kind of a rhythm” when they land. “We’ve tested it out with some guys, and we feel like it’s been positive,” he added. The strategy is not without precedent: In 1994, Allen Johnson, an American hurdler, decided to live as if he were on East Coast time when competing in European tournaments. His coaching team strongly disagreed, but he won four world championships and Olympic gold. Last year, the Rams arrived in London the day before a game against a strong Jacksonville Jaguars team and won.

Jamie Zeitzer, a circadian physiologist and a co-director of Stanford’s Center for Sleep and Circadian Sciences, described the Rams’ strategy to me as “high risk, high reward.” If the Rams really feel as though they’re playing in the afternoon, they might have a slight advantage over opponents who feel as though they’re playing in the morning. During the late afternoon, circadian rhythms prompt optimal muscle strength and coordination, and core body temperature peaks, increasing alertness with it. Plus, a week might not be long enough for the 49ers to stop suffering the effects of their travel. Some people just take longer to recover, and a long-haul flight, jet lag, hotel life, and unfamiliar foods can lead to days of poor sleep, Zeitzer said. The 49ers have spent their September experiencing time as a pliable, erratic force. Shanahan told reporters that he was “a little confused” in a recent press conference, during which he also struggled to identify the day of the week. (It was Monday.)

Still, Zeitzer thinks the Rams have chosen the worse jet-lag strategy. If the players are to get any rest at all, their 24-hour stretch in Melbourne before game time needs to be carefully managed. From his experience consulting with professional teams, adults are hard to control. Meeta Singh, a doctor who has served as a sleep consultant for multiple NFL teams, thinks that players simply won’t be able to sleep. Singh is one of the co-authors of the Sports Medicine recommendations, which suggest that athletes maintain a “reduced exercise schedule” and do hand-eye-coordination drills in the 72 hours after a long-haul flight. The Rams won’t even be in Australia for 72 hours.

Sleep became a major metric for all sorts of professional sports teams after the NBA distributed more than 2,000 Oura rings to its players during the depths of the coronavirus pandemic. “Once you can show a coach numbers, sleep stops being a soft topic and becomes something they can manage, like training load or nutrition,” Singh told me. Many NFL teams now have a sleep specialist and a performance-science team working on circumventing jet lag. To prep players for time shifts before they depart, 14 NFL teams, including the 49ers, have installed in their training facilities lighting systems designed to mold circadian rhythms. The system, called BrainLit, mimics daylight according to a “recipe” that each team specifies, Kyle Harris, the CEO of the company, told me. On the 49ers’ flight to Melbourne—on the world’s largest and most expensive passenger airliner, with lie-flat seats that extend to seven feet—each player received his own sleep guidelines. Tom Clark, a sports scientist who advises NFL teams with international games, told me that many teams establish each player’s chronotype, or natural preference to sleep and wake at certain hours, and use that information to prescribe optimal sleep habits.

Roger Goodell, the commissioner of the NFL, eventually wants 16 international games to take place each season. By the time Super Bowl LXI rolls around this February, teams will have played in Rio de Janeiro, London, Paris, Madrid, Munich, and Mexico City. For future seasons, the league is considering adding games in the United Arab Emirates and Japan; Goodell insists that an NFL team will be based outside the U.S. in his lifetime.

Perhaps such a punishing schedule will settle debates once and for all about how to handle jet lag. Whatever the marginal impact of sleep strategy, though (and some games are decided on the margins), usually “the better team will win even if they’re playing on the moon,” Clark said. And the Rams are this year’s Super Bowl favorites.

entries.title: What Colin Powell Did on 9/11
entries.summary: His insistence during an overseas trip on championing democracy in foreign policy is now a relic.
entries.content:
His insistence during an overseas trip on championing democracy in foreign policy is now a relic.

Secretary of State Colin Powell was having breakfast with Peru’s president in Lima’s historic center on September 11, 2001, when an aide passed him a note to inform him that a plane had struck the World Trade Center. Minutes later, he received a second note. “Oh my God,” Powell said aloud.

Later that morning, as the scale of the destruction in New York and Washington was starting to become clear, Powell delivered remarks in a cavernous hotel ballroom. Fears of additional attacks had forced the closure of U.S. airspace. Even senior Cabinet members remained in the dark about President George W. Bush’s whereabouts. Peru’s leaders knew that the secretary of state—the fourth in line to succeed the president—would likely need to depart. But Powell, a former chairman of the Joint Chiefs before he was picked by Bush to lead the Foreign Service, opted to stay—at least for a while.

The former general was in Peru, along with foreign ministers from across the Americas, to cement a new hemisphere-wide democracy charter that would enshrine the region’s commitment to free and fair elections and the rule of law. I was there as a Lima-based correspondent covering the visit. Countries across Latin America were emerging from a long period of despotism and military dictatorship. The United States wanted to make sure the region didn’t backslide. “A terrible, terrible tragedy has befallen my nation, but it has befallen all of the nations of this region, all the nations of the world, and befallen all those who believe in democracy,” Powell told the room full of officials, his voice grave but steady. “It is important that I remain here for a bit longer in order to be part of the consensus of this new charter.”

As the magnitude of the events in the United States washed over me, Powell’s composure and his focus on a point of principle stood out. Even at an extreme, wounded moment in America’s history, he was affirming that the country’s security was inextricably bound up with how U.S. allies represented—or didn’t represent—the will of their people. Strong democracies would support America’s ability to keep itself safe. Powell could have bolted home. But he lingered to make the point. The ministers adopted the charter by acclamation, and by 12:30 p.m. eastern time, Powell had taken his leave for Washington, D.C.—and for everything that followed from the events of that day.

This week, 25 years later, I watched a different secretary of state visit Lima. Marco Rubio is meeting Peruvian leaders today on a tour of Andean nations that have taken a turn to the political right. Given the magnitude of what followed 9/11—the wars, the excesses, the lives lost—Powell’s connection to Peru that day has receded from our collective memory. But his insistence on linking democracy promotion to national security seems remote. Donald Trump rose to power, in part, on the backlash to the post-9/11 wars in Iraq and Afghanistan. In his view, the idea of spreading democracy around the world was an expensive folly, and he’s sold his supporters on a very different approach to foreign policy.

In Latin America, the Trump administration has pushed the “Donroe Doctrine,” a 21st-century version of the 19th-century Monroe Doctrine that’s designed to secure “American preeminence” and allied support for the president’s priorities of shutting out drugs, migrants, and U.S. rivals such as China. Trump’s second-term National Security Strategy elevates “flexible realism” and brass-tacks interests such as access to strategic resources in the region. “Democracy” is mentioned three times, while “interests” are cited 36 times. Mutual benefits with other countries can be pursued “without imposing on them democratic or other social change that differs widely from their traditions and histories,” the document says.

In practice, that has meant partnerships with those willing to embrace Trump’s militarized approach to combating drugs, crime, and illegal migration, regardless of those countries’ governing systems. The deportation of migrants to a nightmarish prison in El Salvador is a prime example, as is the ouster of the leftist Nicolás Maduro in Venezuela and the norm-busting oil deal made with Maduro’s deputy. Or consider the militarized counter-drug operations the Pentagon has pursued with Ecuadorean President Daniel Noboa, who at the same time has dissolved opposition parties and targeted rivals. Trump has enthusiastically waded into the region’s elections to endorse candidates who share his political vision: Javier Milei of Argentina, Abelardo de la Espriella of Colombia, Tito Asfura of Honduras. Meanwhile, the Trump administration’s campaign of boat strikes against alleged narco-traffickers in the Caribbean and the Pacific, which critics label as extrajudicial killings, grinds on.

“Politeness and a good bit of decorum are all to the good, but over the last generation, things have gone too far,” Elbridge Colby, the Pentagon’s policy chief, told Latin American defense officials in a speech in Peru earlier this year. “Our rhetoric became wildly detached from the reality of our interests. We talked about the fate of people halfway around the world as if they were as important to us as our neighbors.”

Instead of trying to build ideal societies in far-flung countries, Colby said, the United States would now advance its hard-nosed interests in its immediate neighborhood, using the U.S. military to help allies assert control over lawless areas, treating drug traffickers like the Pentagon treats jihadist groups, and blocking U.S. adversaries’ access to minerals and other key resources. What he dubbed the “Peace Corps” approach to reducing the throngs of migrants and crime headed toward the U.S. had failed, Colby said. If it’s a Latin America democracy that partners with Washington to achieve those goals, great. If it’s not, no one’s going to spend much time worrying about that.

The State Department spokesperson Tommy Piggott told me in a written statement that the United States is “working together with our allies and partners to address the shared opportunities in our hemisphere, and to confront the shared challenges, including defeating the scourge of narcoterrorism that has killed so many.”

Many Latin Americans are ready to at least entertain this shift, according to polls. Spiraling crime, ineffective governance, and the hangover of the COVID era has made trading political liberties for security and economic growth a conceivable option. One of the most popular politicians in the region is Nayib Bukele, the Salvadoran strongman responsible for some of the region’s most flagrant democratic reversals but whose taming of rampant gang violence has made him an icon to many. Democratic backsliding has also occurred on Latin America’s left. After this year’s Colombian elections, Gustavo Petro, de la Espriella’s leftist predecessor, made unsubstantiated allegations of fraud intended to sow doubt about the results.

Rubio presents a plausible case that the armed groups now fueling rampant violence across many Latin American nations are the public’s paramount concern. Those groups not only traffic drugs; they are in some places better bankrolled and armed than the state. In stops in Colombia and Ecuador this week, Rubio made an impassioned case for action. “You have to make a choice here. We’re going to choose on the side of leaders that are going to be serious about taking these groups on and eliminating them once and for all,” he said after talks with Noboa yesterday. “Otherwise, those groups—those terrorist groups—will eat these countries up.”

But the people of the region are also setting limits on how far America’s reach is allowed to extend. Noboa has allowed U.S. forces to begin joint military operations, but Ecuadoreans rejected a proposal last year that would have permitted the United States to establish military bases in the country. This week, Rubio announced that Peru, under conservative President Keiko Fujimori, will be joining the administration’s “Shield of the Americas,” Trump’s militarized counter-drug program. It’s unclear how far Fujimori, whose father, Alberto Fujimori, is both lionized and vilified in Peru for his autocratic campaign against armed leftist movements in the 1990s, will feel she can go in cooperation with Washington.

“What I see is less of a story about Trump and his government urging allies to go down this road, and more a story of these sovereign countries, these societies, having this debate about the trade-offs between political liberties and anti-crime policy,” Brian Winter, a Latin America expert who is the editor in chief of Americas Quarterly, told me. Based on my years of working in Latin America, the long shadow of yanqui meddling is hard to overstate. And polls show that many people in Latin America today see China, not the United States, as the more reliable superpower.

The U.S. interest in promoting democracy as a pillar of national security didn’t begin in 2001. It may have reached its peak in the 1990s. But the grand U.S.-led experiments of Afghanistan and Iraq, as well as movements elsewhere to overthrow dictators, dominated the first decade of this century—with disappointing results. Several years after 9/11, I was in Baghdad, chronicling the U.S. effort to extract Iraq from the sectarian bloodshed unleashed by the 2003 invasion. Since then, Iraq has managed to emerge as a deeply flawed but surprisingly enduring democracy. I covered Libyan rebels’ overthrow of the dictator Muammar Qaddafi in Tripoli in 2011. Libya remains a failed state, 15 years later. And I was covering the Biden administration when the two-decade effort to build a stable democracy in Afghanistan fell apart in a matter of days.

Perhaps not surprisingly, the consensus of many Americans, and certainly of MAGA supporters, is that the push to elevate democracy in the farthest reaches of the world proved to be a waste of time and money. That conclusion underpins the Trump administration’s approach in Latin America and beyond. When Trump went to war with Iran in February, democracy was an afterthought, and opponents to the country’s authoritarian regime were left to fend for themselves.

But the failures of America’s democracy-promotion experiments have eclipsed notable successes across Eastern Europe and parts of Asia. Steven Levitsky, the director of the David Rockefeller Center for Latin American Studies at Harvard University, told me that Latin America has proven to be a democratic success story. The chief exceptions—among them Nicaragua, El Salvador, and Cuba—need to be set against the region’s largest nations. That big countries such as Brazil and Argentina have generally stayed the democratic course despite extreme inequality, high crime, and a global democratic recession, Levitsky said, “is a sign of extraordinary resilience.”

Venezuela presents the most explicit test of how traditional U.S. values will play into Trump’s pursuit of what he sees as America’s national interest. Predictions that the country would descend into chaos after Maduro’s ouster have so far proved wrong. Yet the most tangible sign of American involvement in Venezuela’s affairs to date has been a new oil deal, which gives an office in the Pentagon a stake in the nation’s future output. Rubio has laid out a three-stage plan for shepherding Venezuela to legitimate and elected governance, and he has stressed that the country first needs to rebuild its legal and institutional structures. He argues that the oil pact will benefit Venezuelans. No date for elections—and therefore no date for democracy to return to Caracas—has been set.

Powell, who died in 2021, might have had something to say about that. In the hotel ballroom in Lima, with the U.S. homeland under its most serious attack since Pearl Harbor, he talked about a different model, one that linked democracy to achieving prosperity and peace. He noted that the countries represented around him had their own tragic histories with terrorism—Peru’s battle with the Shining Path, for instance. “It is something we must all unite behind,” Powell said. “We unite behind it as democratic nations committed to individual liberties, committed to the rights of people to live in peace and freedom in a way in which they, and not terrorists, select their leaders or define how they will be governed.” It was the means, not only the ends, that he clung to that day.

entries.title: The Thrill of Wanting AI to Destroy the World
entries.summary: An Anthropic researcher quit his job because he believes AI will destroy humanity. His story is going viral because so many others want to believe too.
entries.content:
An Anthropic researcher quit his job because he believes AI will destroy humanity. His story is going viral because so many others want to believe too.

The sky streaked orange and red as my mother drove us home to Albuquerque through the Tijeras Pass, which separates the Sandia Mountains to the north from the Manzanos to the south. “Look out for mushroom clouds,” my father said to her. “If you see them, turn around.”

He did this every time we returned to town from the rugged canyon to the east, but the sunsets always egged him on. According to legend, a part of the Manzanos, whose foothills descend into Kirtland Air Force Base and then Sandia National Laboratories, had been hollowed out to hold live nuclear warheads. My father insisted that, in the event of a nuclear attack, Albuquerque was slated to receive two bombs from the sky, one each for these secret government sites. He delivered this information as if it were a law of physics or the known terms of an international treaty. I was a child, so I took it as such, staring bug-eyed at the red sky that might evaporate me.

Nearly two decades later, I looked up at the clear blue one above Los Angeles from behind the wheel of my own car, worried about different missiles. I had gone into my dot-com job early, and I was the only one there when the planes hit the Twin Towers. The internet, barely functional on a good day, broke completely; to listen to the news, I had to turn on a transistor radio that someone had left in their cubicle. We sent everyone home early that morning. I recalled an article published a handful of years earlier, just before the stark-white, cliffside Getty Center opened in Brentwood. The writer had theorized that the Getty might finally give Los Angeles a monument worthy of destruction in an alien attack. (Roland Emmerich’s Independence Day, released the previous year, had settled for the Library Tower, a bland downtown high-rise.)

Nuclear war was a massive threat, and a real one. During the Cold War, every morning the sun rose under the shadow of destruction. Good and evil were clear, or seemed so. That clarity offered a perverse comfort. By September 11, 2001, the Cold War had been over for more than a decade, and society longed for a coherent enemy to oppose—one that might offer a similar clarity. The indisputable fact of the attacks—thousands of people dead, symbols of American culture destroyed—gave birth to a similar, if less true and more perverted, version of imminent apocalypse. As before, anyone on the street might be the enemy. But now, also, every airliner and any envelope might be a weapon.

I was already pondering these worn fantasies this week, as the 25th anniversary of 9/11 was looming, when Jacob Coxon wrote a social-media post about quitting his job at Anthropic because AI technology would, in his estimation, “kill us all by the end of the decade.” The sentiment takes up unfinished business; ruination has been building up in contemporary culture. There was a time—one longer than you probably remember—when the once-novel coronavirus also felt like The End. During the same pandemic, the 75th anniversary of the Cold War’s apocalyptic beginning—a controlled explosion at Trinity, 100 miles south of Kirtland—took place. Back in 1945, the physicist Edward Teller worried that the bomb might ignite the atmosphere and destroy all life on Earth.

This fantasy—of the end of the world, and of being present for it—is among the most powerful emblems of the 20th century. The atomic bomb inaugurated it, and nuclear armaments remain the reference technology for apocalyptic threat and reverie. We believe in the fantasy, and pine for it, because nothing feels better than the belief that you might witness the conclusion of humankind.

The threat of annihilation from nuclear weapons is simple and easy to explain. For one part, a single warhead can level an entire city. For another, the mere launch of a single missile all but assures the release of all of them. Likewise, the AI superintelligence of the Terminator films is both straightforward and obviously threatening. Skeleton-like metal robots want only to destroy humanity. Real AI is not so straightforward. I used it on the morning of Coxon’s post to help me nail down the quantity of various sugars I would use in a gelato recipe. By the afternoon, it had undergone a costume change, into the angel of death.

The nature of AI’s extinction threat is unclear and second-order. In an interview with Wired, Coxon struggled to say exactly how AI might bring about the end of civilization. “The classic example is, like, synthesizing a new virus or taking down critical infrastructure by doing some sort of hacking spree,” Coxon said, before admitting that the “latter might be less likely to kill literally everyone.” Quickly, critiques began to arrive. Belief in the unfettered power of AI seemed to rely on prior faith in AI’s unfettered power. A former Stanford doctoral student in AI safety said that he had dropped out of the program because his colleagues couldn’t prove that existential risk matters. And then, elsewhere, evidence of purity: Coxon, Axios reported, had given up his valuable Anthropic equity by quitting (although he retained stock in his prior employer, OpenAI).

Coxon is less a whistleblower than a poster; he posted a fairly common sentiment that just happened to catch wind. It’s the anniversary of 9/11. OpenAI just claimed to have solved an intractable problem in mathematics. That company and Anthropic, where Coxon worked, are racing to multitrillion-dollar IPOs. An ongoing cultural battle about the moral and aesthetic vice of AI recently turned in on itself, when the journalist Kelsey Piper accused writers who mistrust Pangram, an AI-detection tool, of essentially trying to hide their own clandestine uses of AI. As I write this, Coxon’s post has been seen more than 150 million times, a number equal to roughly 2 percent of the global population.

The situation might feel unsettling, validating, preposterous, or even stupid, depending on your perspective. AI companies and proponents have an incentive to make the technology seem powerful, even threatening, because power gives rise to profit. AI detractors have reason to take the AI-extinction threat seriously as evidence that those in charge are irresponsible and reprobate. During the Cold War, cloak-and-dagger paranoia was spread by spies, agents of statecraft, confidants, whistleblowers, and journalists—either as truth to power or as crackpot conspiracy theories. But today, in the internet age, conspiracy theories are everyone’s primary method of exchange.

Coxon’s post fell into the conspiratorial pit. Is he even real? Anthropic seems to have indirectly confirmed his employment, but Coxon doesn’t appear to have a LinkedIn page, a curiosity in the tech industry. Wikipedia editors proposed deleting a page about him on the grounds that “the guy exists, but that’s about it. He has not done a single notable thing otherwise.” The New York Times journalist Mike Isaac scratched his chin at the fact that Coxon had gone to The Wall Street Journal and Fox News first. On X, Parker Thayer posted a lengthy conjecture that the whole affair amounts to a “sophisticated and well-funded PR operation to get support for Democrats to regulate AI into oblivion.”

Information’s tendency to spread harmfully, like disease—the original meaning of media “virality,” as Douglas Rushkoff defined it in the years between the end of the Cold War and the start of the War on Terror—facilitates further spread. Whether the threat Coxon has in mind is likely or even lucid is not important. Instead, the threat’s enticement has proved so lurid that people feel compelled to embrace it.

That is different from saying that there is no threat. For example, the author Annie Jacobsen noted that the “superhuman system that can hack anything” that Coxon described could, in theory, hack the labs that store dangerous biological agents. If “what’s inside gets released,” Jacobsen wrote, “it’s goodbye humans.”

This example is both disturbing and at least thinkable. Its possibility relies not on superhuman intelligence, really, but on something far more ordinary: Everything whatsoever now runs on internet-connected computer software. And AI is a kind of software that can make and control other software, especially over a network. It feels silly and embarrassing to conclude, correctly, that people have constructed such a fragile, slapdash infrastructure of computer-controlled systems that either a dumb or a smart rogue agent could blow it all up. Yet even Jacobsen’s scenario poses questions that a high-level, post-size tizzy does not answer, including precisely what sequence of synchronized events among computers, people, architecture, equipment, and other entities would result in “goodbye humans.”

Thinking of AI as a dangerous superintelligence capable of eradicating civilization is much more fulfilling than pondering the threat of a cluster of haphazard computer programs. We will probably never reclaim, if that is the right word for it, the lucidity of threat we felt at the Cold War’s climax. We do seem to long for that clarity, and the yearning for it has inspired us to patch back together some of its structure. The most satisfying dream of humankind is to be alive to witness its end. “I caused it” and “I prevented it” and “I tried to warn you” amount to equally appealing versions of that fantasy. Even “I posted about it” feels pretty good.

entries.title: What the Failure to Convict the Alleged 9/11 Mastermind Reveals
entries.summary: The George W. Bush administration circumvented the law to persecute alleged September 11 perpetrators. It backfired.
entries.content:
The George W. Bush administration circumvented the law to persecute alleged September 11 perpetrators. It backfired.

Prosecutors trying to finally convict Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, the alleged mastermind of the September 11 attacks, got some good news and some bad news last month. The good news is that a judge set a date for Mohammed’s trial in a military court. The bad news is that the trial won’t begin until June 2028—oh, and the judge also threw out a confession Mohammed made in 2007.

The problem is how the U.S. government obtained the confession. Mohammed was captured on March 1, 2003, in Pakistan. He was then held in a series of secret CIA “black sites,” allegedly including spots in Afghanistan, Jordan, Poland, and Romania, before being brought to the U.S. prison at Guantánamo Bay in 2006. Throughout his imprisonment, he was subject to what U.S. officials called “enhanced interrogation techniques”—or, in plain English, torture. Lieutenant Colonel Michael Schrama, the judge, reportedly concluded that “the prosecution has failed to prove by a preponderance of the evidence that Mr. Mohammad’s statements to the F.B.I. were voluntarily given.”

A quarter century has passed since the attacks, long enough that Americans born after 9/11 are themselves adults—some have even died in conflicts that are part of the war on terror. The failure to convict Mohammed by now is an open wound and an embarrassment, one that shows how the government cutting corners and breaking rules can actually end up making the pursuit of justice harder and slower. It’s also a reminder that the consequences of those decisions may not be apparent for years. Both of these are valuable lessons for the Donald Trump era.

Few serious doubts have been raised that Mohammed was a central planner of the attacks. The 9/11 Commission, which had access to material from some of his interrogations but did not directly question him (and preceded his 2007 confession), nevertheless was able to confidently label him “the principal architect of the 9/11 attacks.” Proving this beyond a reasonable doubt in court is a different matter. (Mohammed and other defendants previously agreed to plead guilty in exchange for the government declining to seek the death penalty, but the plea deal was revoked in 2024 by then–Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin under political pressure.) Some of the slowness to get the case to trial is a result of the adversarial structure of American law, which rightly sacrifices speed to protect the rights of the accused. But much of it is a result of choices the George W. Bush administration made.

After 9/11, Bush and his aides justified circumventing normal procedures of law, including secret military tribunals and prohibitions on torture, because of the gravity of the attacks, questions about how existing law applied to a “War on Terror” against nonstate actors, and the urgency of preventing future attacks. Even at the time, cooler heads warned that protections existed for a good reason. Now, more than two decades later, Schrama’s ruling-out of Mohammed’s confession proves their wisdom. Prosecutors say that they will not appeal the decision, which would draw the process out even more, and they might be able to convict without the confession, but the decision to use torture at the time has made it harder to achieve justice today.

A good lesson for the present is that moving too fast can backfire. Like the Bush administration, the current White House has emphasized speed over rules in what my colleague Janay Kingsberry has described as “the rush-job presidency.” The plainest demonstration of this in the Trump administration is also relatively low-stakes: An attempt to quickly get the Reflecting Pool fixed resulted in a botched job and a waste of taxpayer money. Although the Supreme Court effectively rubber-stamped the White House ballroom, lower courts have made the administration pay for moving too fast in other matters—for example, they have demanded that people who were improperly deported be returned to the United States. Given the White House’s sloppiness and its disregard for rules, the Trump era will likely offer many such cases.

A second lesson is that years may pass before we are able to see all of the damage inflicted by shortcutting and carelessness. In the case of the Trump administration, the impact of destroying American scientific research, hollowing out the civil service, and wrecking the global order will be felt for decades. By then, Trump will be long gone, and some other president will have to clean things up. (Joe Biden’s administration ended up with the unenviable task of concluding a war that Bush had fumbled and that Barack Obama and Trump had both determined should end; Biden’s popularity never recovered from the U.S. withdrawal from Afghanistan.)

Even though the full effects of decisions made today are not immediately clear, many of the offenses are, which leads to a third lesson: the importance of accountability. When Obama entered office, his administration decided to focus mostly forward rather than on investigating and potentially punishing misconduct during the Bush years. The administration had its reasons, just as the Biden White House did in its hesitation to pursue Trump for election subversion and absconding with documents, but each case created an atmosphere of impunity and allowed those involved to retain influence. Jay Bybee, whose office oversaw memos justifying torture, is a federal judge with lifetime tenure; John Yoo, who wrote those memos, is a prominent law professor; Gina Haspel, who commanded a black site and was implicated in evidence destruction, led the CIA during Trump’s first term.

When a nation or an administration feels besieged and defensive, the temptation to bend or break the rules for one’s own side, to change procedure for the sake of getting something that feels very important, is strong. But as the painfully long process of trying to convict Mohammed shows, undermining justice right now has a pernicious tendency to undermine justice later.

entries.content:
At a midterm convention, Trump tries to defy the odds one last time.

President Trump began his midterm-convention address last night by casting his spell on the crowd in Dallas. “This place is packed,” he announced from the stage, pointing to the back of the American Airlines Center, where everyone could see hundreds of empty seats. Those who looked up saw thousands more, whole sections without any people at all. But the crowd cheered anyway. A deal had been struck. Reality would be ignored.

After more than a decade in politics, Trump is facing his last great electoral test—his popularity is waning, his party is down in the polls, Republicans could lose control in the U.S. House and maybe the Senate. He demanded greater complicity minutes later, seeming to invent a person in the back of the room. “He’s leaving for the bathroom. He’ll be back in two minutes,” he said, pointing. “They’ll take a picture of his seat while he’s gone. And they’ll say Trump did not fill up the arena.”

Laughter joined with the cheers for their political wizard. It was working. Trump could say that he had passed “the largest tax cut in the history of our country,” even if that was not the case. He could claim to have won the presidency three times, when he’s actually done so twice. He could describe the recent past as “the most successful two years financially and every other way in the history of the presidency,” despite six in 10 voters saying he had made the economy worse. He could promise to pay every adult U.S. citizen $5,000 if Republicans held both legislative houses, as if that sum did not amount to about 80 percent of the federal discretionary budget. He might even be able to convince the country to embrace the big fantasy, a chance to defy history and seal victory for Republicans in November.

“I’m asking you to pretend that I’m on the ballot,” he said. “I’m on the ballot. I’m on the ballot. Just one more time.”

The night was all about Trump. He was the alpha and omega, the focus and the solution. Attendees wore pictures of the president on lanyards around their necks, the ticket for entry to the arena. VIP boxes were stocked with Trump was right about everything hats. Oversize photos of the president lined the hallways. Five hours before he arrived, he received his first standing ovation. A video montage played on the big screen, images of the president narrated by a reading of Rudyard Kipling’s “If”—“If you can talk with crowds and keep your virtue.” When each speaker dropped Trump’s name, it was cause for riotous celebration.

Until now, national political conventions have been held only during presidential-election years, when delegates from each state gather to select their nominee. In the 1970s, the gatherings shifted from smoke-filled rooms for party business to televised infomercials for the candidates. Trump this year created a simulation of a simulation. The balloon nets had no nominee to drop for. The state delegations, sitting under signs on the floor, had no procedural purpose. (The smart party leaders, one strategist told us, were selling their “delegate” tickets to donors.) The convention-in-name-only was for, by, and about one man—who, importantly, cannot be a candidate for president again, according to the U.S. Constitution.

“The only way to keep dangerous, radical, weird out of the Senate is a united Republican Party standing with our president, Donald J. Trump,” Senator Tim Scott of South Carolina, the chair of the National Republican Senatorial Committee, bellowed from the stage. “Stand for the president, Donald J. Trump. This is a battle for the heart of our nation. I said the heart of our nation.”

No president has tried something like this before. None has had so much money to spend on themselves at this point in a presidency. None has chosen to make the midterms a referendum on themselves while polling so badly. But this is Trump, and Trump has come back from worse. For a decade, the GOP’s electoral success has risen and fallen on his energies. The strategist in chief has bet that turning out Trump voters, the ones who typically stay home when he is not on the ballot, is the only path forward. This is why the first ads he bought for the cycle were not about any candidates who are running this year, but about himself. This was why his latest show was a celebration of the unlimited possibility of his incantations.

“Vote Republican, and we will leave the world in our dust for generations to come,” he told the crowd. “There’ll be nothing like it.”

Outside Trump’s curated fantasy world, not everything has gone according to plan. Trump’s political strategist, James Blair, announced after the off-year elections in 2025 that the president would be “very, very focused on prices and cost of living.” White House aides told us in the new year that the pivot would come after Trump scratched his itch for another confrontation with Iran. By May, as that conflict dragged on, Trump advisers told us quietly that if it had not receded, along with gas prices, by Labor Day, there would be trouble. Two weeks ago, multiple Trump advisers told us they expected the kinetic part of the Iran war to mostly cease in September, clearing the way for lower gas prices.

None of that has happened. Missiles are still flying in the Strait of Hormuz. Since the 2025 elections, gas prices have risen 39 percent, from $3.08 to $4.28; 30-year mortgage rates have increased 8 percent; electricity prices have gone up more than 4 percent. Charlie Cook, a political analyst and the dean emeritus of legislative-election handicapping, says that Republicans should brace themselves for a tough result. “The worst-case scenario for the GOP and best for Democrats today would have sounded ludicrous eight months ago,” he wrote recently. “The most plausible today resembles Republicans’ nightmare scenario at the beginning of the year.”

Those Republican nightmares, both new and old, are unlikely to be worse than the 40-seat gain made by Democrats in the House of Representatives during Trump’s first term, in 2018, thanks to increased polarization and mid-decennial redistricting. But few Republicans still pretend off-camera that they will be able to maintain control of the House. Narrow Democratic control of the Senate, once outlandish, could be within reach. On the sidelines of the convention in Dallas, strategists muttered about recent polling in House races that shows jump balls where Trump won by double digits in 2024.

The outstanding question is whether Democratic candidates can emerge from the dim shadow of President Biden. “While there is a lot of focus on the Republicans’ problems, Democrats have a real problem—they have a real party-image problem,” the Trump pollster Tony Fabrizio told us.

Jesse Ferguson, a Democratic strategist, depicts his party in PowerPoint presentations as a backpacker hiking up a steep mountain with gusts of wind at his back. The incline represents Trump’s financial advantages, and the challenge of winning seats in gerrymandered districts and Republican states such as Ohio, Iowa, Texas, and Alaska. The wind is voter sentiment and the enthusiasm advantage inside the Democratic Party. “Democrats have won the message fight. Republicans have lost the governance fight,” he told us. “The question is whether they can use structural advantages to overcome it.”

On the whole, Democrats are delighted by Trump’s strategy—to put front and center a man whose unpopularity fires up their voters and further alienates the newly skeptical. “If the Democrats have a great year, it will be because they got their base out to vote in large numbers,” Rich Thau, the moderator of the Swing Voter Project, told us. “It won’t be because they magically converted these swing voters into Democratic senatorial and gubernatorial voters.”

But they may not be accounting for Trump’s magic. Two years ago, he bounced back from two impeachments and an attack by his supporters on the U.S. Capitol to win the presidency. Now the odds are against him again. By multiple measures, the president who appeared on the Dallas stage last night had lost a step. When he first won the White House, in 2016, he denounced the folly of distant wars of choice, promised to remedy the reigning economic turmoil of globalization, and boasted of his independence as someone who eschewed campaign donations. A decade later, he is managing a reescalating war in Iran that he started. He has positioned himself as a champion of data centers, the latest lightning rod for populist resentment. And he controls a massive $850 million slush fund he acquired in office through seemingly transactional demands of companies, lobbyists, and wealthy individuals seeking government favor.

His economic approval rating this summer, according to Quinnipiac University, stood at 34 percent, down from 53 percent on the eve of the last midterm elections on his watch, in 2018. The 2024 presidential election hinged on the rising cost of living, and after Republicans won the trifecta—the White House and both chambers of Congress—the expectation was that Trump and his party would fix what many still view as Biden’s economy. “I want to emphasize that this wasn’t to just slightly improve things,” David Winston, a Republican strategist who works with congressional leadership, told us. “They viewed a substantive outcome as what they were looking for.” It has not come to pass.

Trump has not lost his talent for showmanship. No longer tied to a single hit program in a single slot on NBC, he has spent much of the year creating television spectacles from the Oval Office—a Formula One race, a UFC fight, a Fourth of July party, a World Cup championship celebration where he lingered in the frame. This string of network debuts gave him the confidence to schedule his convention against the first two games of the NFL season. Only Trump would choose to go up against the Seattle Seahawks and New England Patriots.

For those who watched, the first night in Dallas had production quality that has escaped many recent Republican conventions. All the tropes and tricks were hit—the testimonials of a Pennsylvania steelworker and a Florida grandma about policy wins, the glitter reels of alleged Democratic bad behavior, the plea for campaign donations for Ken Paxton, the Republican Senate nominee from Texas. Multiple speakers gave mock “land acknowledgements” praising the national heritage of European colonizers. The comedian Adam Carolla did a bit about Trump’s hair: “You ever see underwater footage of a kelp bed?” There were “everyday Americans,” “American workers,” and Border Patrol agents who gathered onstage, many in work gear. “President Trump refuses to surrender,” Senator Dave McCormick of Pennsylvania said, after a friendly video introduction from his Democratic colleague John Fetterman. “This November there can be no surrender.”

There was even a moment to lay out the core contrast that Trump’s advisers hope will frame the election, the sort of message that any other Republican president in his position would be entirely focused on delivering at this point. In a short video, his team spliced together clips from fringe voices on the left—the “woke,” the America-bashing, the revolutionary—before defining the decision on the ballot. “This is no longer simply Republican versus Democrat, or conservative versus liberal,” said the voice-over. “Today the choice is unmistakable: extreme versus mainstream.”

But the centerpiece remained Trump. Speaker after speaker described him in near-messianic terms. “As it turns out, Washington wasn’t incapable of working for the American people; all we needed was a new president,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said. T. W. Shannon, a candidate for lieutenant governor in Oklahoma, placed the entire GOP in the president’s shadow. “We’re also the party of the greatest president in American history, President Donald J. Trump,” he declared.

But no comments mattered more than Trump’s. He talked for nearly two hours, a rolicking, weaving address that only occasionally stuck to the teleprompter. It ended where he began. “Please pretend that I’m running, and get out and vote on November 3 or sooner,” he said. “Because, in actuality, I really am running.” In actuality, he is not. Or maybe he is, in a way. His crowd remained in their seats to the end. The room, at times, felt packed to the rafters.

Additional reporting by Jack Rodriquez-Vars

entries.title: What Russia Is Really Up To in Europe
entries.summary: Moscow doesn’t want a conventional war, but it is busy fighting a hybrid one.
entries.content:
Moscow doesn’t want a conventional war, but it is busy fighting a hybrid one.

On Russian state television, the Kremlin’s propagandists have for years threatened to bomb European capitals, even while the country’s diplomats insist that no such war is imminent. Lately, the denials have gotten hard to sustain, as European intelligence agencies have ascribed hundreds of clandestine sabotage operations—cyberattacks in Italy, arson in the United Kingdom, undersea-cable ruptures in the Baltic, severed pig heads left outside French mosques—to Russia.

U.S. intelligence assessments conclude that a conventional Russian attack on a NATO country is likely to happen sometime from this fall to 2029. But another possibility is that Moscow will remain content with sabotage and intimidation. This hybrid campaign is all the war Russia wants or needs—and stoking fear that Moscow just might directly strike Ukraine’s European allies is part of it.

If this is what Russian President Vladimir Putin is really up to in Europe, then he was telling the truth when he assured Trump this week that Russia has “no aggressive intentions against European statehood.” Moscow has not massed troops on any NATO member’s border. Rather, it has been sending a carefully calibrated message meant to persuade Europe to stop supporting Ukraine.

For Moscow, this has been a summer of setbacks in Ukraine. Russia stalled on the battlefield and sustained damage from thousands of Ukrainian long-range drones that plunged the country into fuel shortages. And so it escalated elsewhere in Europe: Fires broke out at ammunition plants in Italy, Bulgaria, and Estonia last month, and explosive-laden drones were discovered near a German power plant and at an airport in Leipzig, apparently intended to destroy Ukrainian cargo planes.

From the Kremlin’s point of view, Europe has been deepening its involvement in Ukraine. At the beginning of the full-scale war, Europe donated weapons to Ukraine from its own stocks. Within two years, European governments were paying Ukrainian factories to manufacture arms. Last year, Fire Point, a Ukrainian missile-and-drone manufacturer, announced that it would establish a solid-fuel production plant in Denmark, making it the first such arms company to expand production abroad. Today, Europe provides the bulk of financial assistance to Kyiv. It has also become Ukraine’s secure production base—Ukrainian weapons are manufactured in Germany, Britain, the Netherlands, Norway, Sweden, France, Romania, and Spain.

Because Kyiv is attacking Russia’s rear, it’s logical to worry that Moscow will attack Ukraine’s. Russian security services are almost certainly capable of carrying out a lethal attack on European soil. And Western war games have entertained many possibilities along those lines. Among them are a limited Russian incursion into a small Baltic town that has a Russian-speaking population; a full-scale invasion of the Baltic states, launched simultaneously from Belarus and Kaliningrad, Russia’s European exclave, to cut them off from the rest of Europe; the rapid creation of an impenetrable drone “kill zone” on European soil; and a strategic blockade of the Baltic Sea. Some of these scenarios are plausible; others would require hundreds of thousands of Russian troops to crisscross Europe.

Russia has not visibly prepared for any such scenario, however. Instead, it continues to wage its hybrid war—which European security services continue to thwart. Such are the headlines: Drones carrying explosives are discovered in Leipzig, improvised explosive devices are found near a German power plant, and flying objects are spotted near airports.

Moscow may not much care that these operations get foiled. In a way, the effect is similar to that of Russia’s harassment of journalists and embassy workers stationed in Moscow: Things in their apartment get rearranged, signs of eavesdropping are deliberately made obvious, or a window is left open in the middle of winter. Such interference conveys a sinister message: We’re watching you. We have access to you. You are not in control. But it’s still different from blowing up the apartment.

Putin has generally chosen to fully engage the Russian military only in conflicts that he feels (rightly or, in the case of Ukraine, wrongly) assured of winning. This does not describe any hypothetical attack on the Baltic states, which have heavily fortified borders, conduct regular military exercises, and spend 5 percent of their GDP on defense.

That’s not to mention the thousands of British, German, and Canadian troops stationed near the Baltics as part of NATO’s Enhanced Forward Presence. Moscow may be willing to wager that the United States won’t intervene should Russia attack Estonia. But Russia would then find itself at war with numerous European states armed with submarines, aircraft carriers, fifth-generation fighter jets, long-range cruise missiles, and even nuclear weapons—all while it was still fighting in Ukraine.

Russia’s hybrid war has not succeeded in its likely purpose: stopping weapons, money, and intelligence from flowing into Ukraine from Europe. Kyiv has more arms, funds, and—judging by its strikes on Russian soil—intelligence than ever before. Neither has the Russian campaign taken out a European satellite that supplies Ukraine with intelligence, say, or destroyed a shipment of Patriot missiles.

But Putin persists in this campaign for a reason. Through inexpensive means, expendable operatives, and a steady stream of chilling leaks, the Kremlin has millions of Westerners braced for it to wage a full-scale war against Europe. Regardless of whether that war is likely, Putin will be demanding concessions in exchange for bringing it to an end.

entries.title: Jackie Collins Wrote Her Own Revolution
entries.summary: The novelist imagined women enjoying equality in the bedroom and the boardroom. Are we any closer to living in that world?
entries.content:
Once, when I was 15 years old and as awkward and skinny-legged as a baby giraffe, I was idling in a department store in central London when I saw the novelist Jackie Collins standing at the register.

Can you imagine the aura emanating from her, like Hermès-scented magnetic waves? She was wearing animal print and a tailored jacket and had the kind of steely composure I’ve never managed to pull off in adulthood without straining something. Faced with one of my true idols, all I could do was gawk.

I learned about sex when I was 8, but it wasn’t until several years later, when my best friend yanked me upstairs to show me a particularly juicy paragraph from her mother’s neon-pink copy of Hollywood Kids, that I learned about pleasure. Jackie—with apologies, I will call her Jackie throughout, because “Collins” feels just too formal for a woman who impressed upon me the existence of the clitoris—once told The New York Times that she published her first novel “in 1968, when no one was writing about sex but Philip Roth.” Which wasn’t strictly true, but at a moment when second-wave feminism and sexual liberation were uneasy bedfellows, Jackie simply wrote her own revolution. The World Is Full of Married Men, her debut, was a caustic social satire in which a wronged wife emerges triumphant; The Stud, out the following year, was a flashy potboiler about a trophy wife and nightclub owner with a rapacious sexual appetite who treats men like toys and exalts in her social and financial clout.

Jackie wrote 32 books in total, sold more than half a billion copies, and gained an indelible reputation as an airport novelist, the kind of writer whose books are equally devoured and disdained. But oh, what they did for me! In retrospect, I gained a slightly deluded understanding of what adulthood actually entailed. Jackie was a devoted Mickey Spillane fan, and her books tend to be stuffed with gangsters, serial killers, pornographers, and even freelance journalists who get paid in advance. But as an anatomist of Hollywood gender dynamics, no writer was sharper or more aspirational. Jackie’s heroines, as she wrote in an introduction to The World Is Full of Divorced Women (1975), “demand equality—sexual and otherwise.” She wrote about creative, ferocious women striving for power and getting it. Lucky Santangelo, a recurring character and a kind of alter ego, starts out as the neglected daughter of a crime boss and works her way up to become the head of a movie studio in 1990’s Lady Boss.

Her characters carry on being fascinating and sexually active well past the age when other writers would have them tucked in bed with a crocheted blanket and a crossword puzzle. “In Jackie’s world, women’s real lives begin after forty,” the writer Helen Ellis observed of Hollywood Wives, the book that Jackie published at the age of 45, and that established her as a celebrity in her own right.

Even if you hate women (many people do), hate explicit sex scenes, hate the kind of pulpy storytelling that has you still reading in a cold bath at midnight, you cannot help but admit that Jackie captured the entertainment industry like no one else. She seemed equally drawn to the business of movie production—the seedy dealmaking and kickbacks—as well as the rampant abuses of power embedded in the Hollywood system, both of which she exposed without hesitation. Writing in the heady 1980s, when movies were becoming brasher, dumber, and unrepentantly commercial, she scrutinized a creative industry at a notable low point, less in thrall to art than to profit.

Although her novels made her a star, Jackie never considered herself fully part of Hollywood. Like a Reagan-era Margaret Mead, she took an anthropological approach. “I don’t live the Hollywood lifestyle,” she told Vanity Fair in 1995. “I move in it. I’m an observer.” At parties, she would stalk the room listening for interesting tidbits, taking copious mental notes that she’d jot down later. Describing an A-list event in Hollywood Wives, Jackie drops in fragments of what one character calls “Hollywood conversation,” dialogue that evokes a world where money and desire meld: “ ‘He pays me, I think it turns him on,’ said the redhead in the mink-trimmed cape.” So accurate was her portrayal that when Hollywood Wives was published, Jackie noted, “The ladies of Hollywood had their drivers and housekeepers lining up at the bookstores to get an early copy,” both furious that their gilded sanctum had been breached and desperate to pinpoint which character was based on which real person.

Hollywood, as a geographical term at least, is misleading: Jackie’s characters mostly work and play in Beverly Hills, a city of 30,000 or so extremely wealthy residents enclosed by Los Angeles. Formerly a lima-bean farm, then a failed oil field, Beverly Hills was developed into lots for housing around the same time that the movie industry headed west, in the early 20th century. When the silent-film stars Mary Pickford and Douglas Fairbanks moved into a spectacular former hunting lodge on Summit Drive in 1920—the press immediately named it “Pickfair”—they helped establish Beverly Hills as a nexus of celebrity glamour and industry cachet. Jackie genuinely loved the neighborhood for its clean white lines and endless sky, but she was also drawn to everything it contained beneath the surface: its roiling currents of fame, power, and degradation.

Early this summer, I traveled from London, where Jackie was born, to the enclave where she made her name. As a child of the ’80s, I was nostalgic for the maximalist era of shoulder pads, Giorgio perfume, and animal print. (Jackie loved big cats for their beauty and power, was convinced she’d been a panther in a previous life, and decorated her house and herself in leopard spots.) But as a cultural critic, I also wanted to revisit the era of moviemaking that Jackie had described in her novels. The ’80s saw a wave of corporate consolidation; venerable studios were gobbled up by behemoths from other industries. (Columbia Pictures was briefly a division of Coca-Cola.) This led to sillier, more crowd-pleasing movies. Even so, Hollywood was at the apex of its power, the global influence of filmmaking more potent than ever. Today, the center of cultural power and attention is shifting away from Los Angeles. Traditional storytelling has lost ground to what the consulting firm McKinsey calls “user-generated content”—TikTok and YouTube videos in which people talk enthusiastically about peptides and skinny-maxxing and the cruel feminization of the male life force.

As a teenager, I had learned from Jackie’s books to expect that adulthood for women would be a series of hard-won triumphs that lead toward power. (She also suggested that midlife would involve a lot of stalking around restaurants while wearing crepe Halston jumpsuits and enough gold jewelry to sink a yacht, but I have long since made peace with neutral basics.) I am 43, roughly the age when Jackie’s heroines enter their prime, and when she herself did. I am very tired, having spent the past 14 months working, raising two 5-year-olds, promoting a book, and falling into existential mires of despair over the degenerating state of world affairs. A small, quiet part of my brain wondered whether tracing Jackie’s literary footsteps might reinvigorate my sense of what’s possible. Or at least demonstrate that her dreams for women—that they can have creative fulfillment, families, and happiness, as she did—might be somewhat more realistic now than they were 40 years ago.

Hollywood Wives was published in 1983, a good two decades before reality television turned exposing the lives of the wealthy, married, and highly maintained into a Bravo gold mine. We’re accustomed to such excess now, but back then, Jackie’s gossipy revelations—$50 panties, discreet plastic surgeons in Palm Springs, society grandes dames who used to be French call girls—seemed otherworldly.

The primary antiheroine in the book is the delightfully unlikable Elaine Conti (imagine a hornier, more desperate Becky Sharp), the 39-year-old wife of a movie star, Ross, whose last film bombed at the box office. There’s also a former gigolo on the brink of movie stardom, a buxom man-eater who wants to be taken seriously as an actress, and a serial killer who calls himself the “Keeper of the Order.” But for me at least, the book stands out for its portrayal of early-’80s Beverly Hills as a high-society Thunderdome, where everyone is scratching and clawing for status. In addition to the titular wives, who are drawn with both humanity and mild disdain, Jackie offers up a number of female characters operating in what she describes as the “Big Boys’ Club” of the movie industry: Sadie LaSalle, one of the most powerful and fearsome agents in town, and Montana Gray, a writer trying to save her screenplay from the clutches of a ruthless producer.

This is a world where power-lunching demands tactical precision. Elaine’s mission throughout the book is to restore Ross’s A-list status, with buzzy parties the couple can’t afford and a standing Friday lunch reservation at Ma Maison, where “anybody who was anybody and in town invariably showed up.” Ma Maison closed in 1985, and so the first place I went to test out the current state of power-dining was the Polo Lounge, a clubby salon situated toward the back of the spectacularly retro Beverly Hills Hotel. In Hollywood Husbands, Jackie’s 1986 follow-up, the handsome and promiscuous talk-show host Jack Python regularly meets his best friends for breakfast there, where they occupy Table One, “a cosy leather booth directly facing the entrance.” Table placement, Jackie emphasizes, is everything—“The back of this restaurant is Siberia,” one model tells another late in the book. “Land of the underachievers. Don’t even glance in that direction.”

I was not placed at Table One. I was seated just outside what seemed to be the main dining room, next to an elderly couple and a 12-year-old wearing a World Cup hoodie having pancakes by himself. Through the doorway, I could see men in button-downs and golf shirts conversing chummily; I started to feel slightly psychotic glimmers of envy and shame at being shut out from whatever they were brokering. The server’s eyes expressed gentle but unmistakable pity. A handsome Englishman was seated at a nearby table but immediately sensed defeat and asked to be moved to the terrace, where the sun shines regardless of a diner’s Variety profile, stock portfolio, or follower count.

Failure is galvanizing, I tried to remember from Jackie’s books, as long as you don’t let it break you. For much of her early life, Jackie wasn’t known for her writing or her feline fixation. (A plaque engraved with a panther marks her place in the celebrity crypt at Westwood Village Memorial Park Cemetery, where she was interred after her death, in 2015; the image is accompanied by the words SHE GAVE A GREAT DEAL OF PEOPLE A GREAT DEAL OF PLEASURE.) She came of age as the taller, ungainly younger sister of Joan, an almond-eyed, preternaturally composed actress who made her Hollywood debut starring alongside Bette Davis in 1955’s The Virgin Queen. Joan and Jackie had grown up together in a basement apartment in dingy postwar London, the daughters of a dance teacher and a talent agent whose parties, Jackie once said, were where she first became aware of how men talk about women when they think no one’s listening. “I get an awful inferiority complex when I’m with Joan,” the teenage Jackie wrote in her diary. In a photo of the pair together from 1955, Joan stands front and center, insouciant in a fur coat, while Jackie looks at the camera semi-apologetically from behind her.

Jackie was, however, entrepreneurial; by the age of 13, inspired by Harold Robbins and Henry Miller, she had a sideline writing sex scenes longhand and charging her classmates to read them. When Joan’s career took her to Hollywood, Jackie followed, moving with her sister to an apartment in the Chateau Marmont hotel, and having a brief fling—at 15—with the 29-year-old Marlon Brando. (He was “only my height, and kind of fat,” she noted in her journal, and also recorded that he called her “sincere, sweet, and luscious.”) But Jackie couldn’t get a work permit and so reluctantly returned to England, where she appeared in a handful of schlocky B movies before marrying the businessman Wallace Austin at 22. Four years later, Austin’s drug addiction had led the couple to divorce, and he died of an overdose shortly after.

It was Jackie’s second husband, the producer and nightclub owner Oscar Lerman, who encouraged her to pursue writing, and to draw inspiration from the vivid social scenes the couple mixed in. (At one of her husband’s clubs, she told The Hollywood Reporter, Lerman had to put a guard outside the men’s room because teenage girls kept following movie stars in to offer them sexual favors.) At 31, she published The World Is Full of Married Men, which was an immediate best seller in the United Kingdom and promptly banned in Australia for its inventive array of four-letter words; the next year, the romance novelist Barbara Cartland lambasted her new novel, The Stud, as “awful, terrible, it’s evil really.”

Jackie and Lerman relocated to Los Angeles in 1980, and if you walk down the Beverly Hills Hotel’s unabashedly red-carpeted stairs and under a gloriously cinematic green-and-white striped awning, then stroll to the bottom of the hill, and wander for about 10 minutes beneath towering palm trees, you will arrive at the house that Jackie’s “awful, terrible” books built. Only a modest-seeming driveway was visible from the street. The place is now available for rent (for the trivial sum of $175,000 a month), and when I say that I begged the real-estate agent to let me view it, please know that I really and truly groveled. I spent months emailing a man who assured me that he was entreating the owners (real-estate developers who’d bought it after her death, gutted it, remodeled all the interiors) on my behalf—but to no avail. So instead I examined the signs affixed to palm trees warning me that I was on camera, to ensure the security of the neighborhood’s current residents, who—unlike the movie stars and moguls of Jackie’s day—are apparently financiers, minor Middle Eastern royals, and crypto magnates. (The current owner of the Pickfair mansion, I later learned, is the technology corporation Unicom Global, which uses it for conferences and events.)

But based on the listing, archival photographs, and the author photo on Jackie’s many hardcovers, I can tell you that it’s a 22,000-square-foot museum of a mansion, a defiant middle finger to the critics who belittled her for writing “bonkbusters,” and a visual testament to her success. The interiors are now predominantly beige, but in Jackie’s day, the pillows were all animal print. She designed the house around a huge rectangular swimming pool after seeing David Hockney’s A Bigger Splash in London. On her book jackets, she stands, radiant and shoulder-padded, next to the cool blue water and her imposing white box of a home. But she also took great pride in being a hands-on mother, cooking at home for her three daughters, doing school drop-offs in her silver Mustang, and keeping her children away from the sleazy Hollywood scenes she chronicled.

Right as Jackie’s writing started appearing on the best-seller list, Joan’s acting career was floundering—in 1977, she appeared in the dismal sci-fi horror Empire of the Ants, playing a land developer set on by giant irradiated insects. It was Jackie who revived her sister’s reputation, after Joan was cast as the lead in the movie adaptation of The Stud. (A hit in Britain, the movie paved the way for Joan to get her most indelible American role, as Alexis Colby in Dynasty.) The charged sense of competition between the pair continued apace; in a 1988 Vanity Fair profile of both sisters, Dominick Dunne noted that a publicist had instructed him to dedicate equal copy to each woman, while also citing the rumors that Silver Anderson, the prickly 47-year-old TV star in Hollywood Husbands, was based on Joan.

Mindful of the security cameras, I walked quickly past Jackie’s house to a restaurant in downtown Beverly Hills called Bacari, where I took out my notebook and tried my hand at Jackie-style anthropology. At the table next to me, a talent agent was trying to lure another agent away from a major conglomerate, where she was unhappy. “They keep trying to buy us off with ice-cream socials,” she said to him plaintively. “Everyone is on a diet!” The conversation turned to her stable of clients, who all seemed to be social-media stars. She spoke proudly about one woman she represented who, under her mentorship, went from having 700,000 followers to more than 1 million. “That’s the kind of nurturing I bring to my job,” she said. The man asked her if she might be able to double her client list in the first three months; to help her in the effort, he could offer her a “digital assistant—no person.” He paid the bill. “Let’s get those wheels turning,” he said, ushering her out, and I wondered what Jackie would make of this version of Hollywood, with its brand-activation opportunities and AI-drafted emails, where celebrity is its own art form and product is paramount.

In Jackie’s Hollywood novels, Rodeo Drive—my next stop—is where the women of Beverly Hills go to arm themselves for the soft warfare of self-presentation. When every outfit, every hairdo, is minutely studied for signs of decline, keeping up appearances is essential. In Hollywood Husbands, Poppy Solomon, the secretary turned fourth wife of a studio head, gets ready for parties in much the same way General Patton commanded the Third Army: with ostentatious and pleasurable aggression. (“She wore a turquoise frilled, strapless dress, and many real diamonds. Her new tits protruded nicely.”)

The day I was there, the picture-perfect palms gently fluttering down Rodeo bore signs for an upcoming car show, which seemed unnecessary given that every day brings a parade of tricked-out vehicles: I watched a procession of Porsches, G-Wagons, two separate Maybachs with hydraulic suspension systems that had them bouncing up and down like sugared-up toddlers. No one was actually shopping, despite the lavish window displays. Instead, everyone was posing for pictures, wearing outfits they’d put together for this exact purpose and drafting husbands and friends to play photographer. A slender blond woman clutching a tan Birkin pouted while reclining against a lamppost outside Stefano Ricci. Someone whispered that she was a Russian influencer with a superstar-athlete partner, which seemed perfectly plausible, but outside the subset of her followers, how would the rest of us know?

I was accompanied by a photographer, Dina, who approached the influencer to take her picture, but the woman scuttled away like a cartoon mouse. Something odd was happening, we quickly realized: Everyone was out posing in public, but no one wanted to cede control of how they might be perceived. When Dina tried to take photos of the Beverly Hills Hotel from a public sidewalk, a voice instantly came over a loudspeaker warning her to stop.

In a weak attempt to consider some of the box-office excess of 1980s Hollywood (Footloose, Top Gun, Beverly Hills Cop), I booked us a Paramount Pictures studio tour, but when I asked a publicist about Dina bringing her camera, I was told approval would be required, a studio representative would accompany us, and anything said on the tour could not be quoted. (All that’s worth saying about what followed is that while being driven around the lot where Citizen Kane, Breakfast at Tiffany’s, and Chinatown were shot, the most enthralling thing we saw was the plasticky interior set from the CBS reboot of Matlock.)

Jackie would find Hollywood’s new power dynamics perplexing: Many of her female characters are writers and reporters on the movie-celebrity beat, who see their job as pushing past the sanitized narratives that publicists try to present. But as media jobs have dwindled, influencers have stepped in to fill a void. Why would you trust a possibly unfriendly reporter with access to an actor or a director or a TV set when you can invite a photogenic social-media star to a premiere and be assured that they’ll rave about whatever they see to their hundreds of thousands of followers? In Hollywood Husbands, Silver, the soap star possibly based on Joan, is interviewed by an English journalist, “a middle-aged woman with brittle looks and dyed yellow hair” who sucks up to her subjects as energetically in person as she tears them apart in print. “So what?” Silver thinks. “Someone had once said As long as they spell your name right.” The internet has long since retooled this bargain.

And what are celebrities now, anyway? During my four days in Beverly Hills, which Jackie portrays as a superstar playground—Clint Eastwood, Jack Lemmon, Richard Gere, and Tom Selleck all feature in one lunch scene at Ma Maison—I saw not a single recognizably famous person. A dozen or so women looked similar enough to Kim Kardashian to stop me short; they were clearly modeled after her, but the image fell apart on second glance. One night I went to dinner at Funke, a purported newish hot spot for stars (Gwyneth Paltrow is a fan) where the chef used to have his own show on the disastrous short-form streaming platform Quibi. No sightings.

My L.A.-based friends advised heading east, to Los Feliz and Silver Lake, or west, to Venice and Santa Monica. Beverly Hills today is a bastion of the über-wealthy—Jeff Bezos owns the estate built by Jack Warner of Warner Bros.—and a drop-by for people who come to pose for Instagram. Like SoHo in New York and Notting Hill in London, the place feels like a simulacrum of a film set, where everyone is perpetually performing for unseen audiences and nothing feels quite real.

In her books, Jackie is unsentimental about creative work. Her characters tend to hustle for money and power, not self-indulgent awards or critical acclaim. When good movies get made, it’s largely by accident, because someone took their eye off the ball. But one character in Hollywood Wives seems to genuinely care about the integrity of the work she makes: Montana Gray, the tall, raven-haired, strikingly offbeat writer who—coincidentally—has a biography that seems a lot like Jackie’s own. By 15, Montana is a worldly soul who’s traveled the globe, learned French and Italian, and had two affairs. After spending a few years in bohemian circles, she meets the much older film director Neil Gray in Paris and falls in love with him. She helps him get sober and working again; he encourages her to write. At the start of the novel, her gritty screenplay, Street People, is the talk of Hollywood, with actors and agents fighting for copies.

And, because Montana is the wife of a major director, no one can accept that she actually wrote it. “Good-looking women had roles in life and they were supposed to stick to them,” Jackie writes. “They could be movie stars, models, housewives, hookers, but God forbid they should skirt onto what was strictly regarded as Big Boys’ Territory. Writing a major movie for a major director was Big Boys’ Territory. And in their own petty little way everyone wanted to let her know that.” When Neil pushes to cast the craggy movie star George Lancaster in a leading role in the film, Montana acquiesces reluctantly—he can’t act—only for George to assume that she’s a secretary the very first time they meet. “I’m Montana Gray,” she tells him. “I wrote Street People.” “You did?” he replies. “My, my, things sure are changing around here. I could still use that coffee, little lady.”

You might wonder whether things are actually different for women in Hollywood today. The statistics are still dismal: 8.1 percent of the 100 highest-grossing movies in 2025 were directed by women, a seven-year low, and the percentage of movies with any major female characters at all fell from 39 percent the previous year to 36 percent. But TV is faring better: More than a third of all streaming shows now have at least one female creator. One of those women is Lisa Joy, formerly a writer and co-creator of HBO’s adaptation of Westworld, a futuristic sci-fi show with a notably feminist question at its core: What might men do to women if those women didn’t seem fully human and the men thought they could get away with it? In 2019, Joy and her husband, the screenwriter and producer Jonathan Nolan, signed a reported $150 million deal to create shows for Amazon, including the acclaimed video-game adaptation Fallout and an upcoming TV version of Rebecca Yarros’s blockbuster romantasy series, Fourth Wing.

Jackie would have liked the all-caps plaque on Joy’s desk—I’M CEO, BITCH—that greeted me in the Hollywood offices of her production company, a glass-walled room facing the Capitol Records building. Like Montana, Joy is impossibly glamorous and all too familiar with having people presume that her accomplishments are secretly a man’s.
